passage: The school hall in Nagpur buzzed as Principal Mr. Deshmukh announced the drawing prize. Irawati's name was read out, and she skipped to the stage. Sarika sat in the third row with her hands clenched in her lap. She had worked on her own peacock for two weeks. Her stomach twisted. Then she pressed her lips together, stood up and clapped hard, and when Irawati came back down she said, “Well done, it's beautiful.” Irawati beamed. At lunch, Sarika sat quietly. She whispered to a friend, “I wanted it too. But I am happy for her.” Her friend squeezed her hand.

qa.q: How long had Sarika worked on her peacock?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling as she clapped for Irawati, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She was disappointed and a little envious, since her hands were clenched and her stomach twisted, yet she chose to celebrate.

qa.q: What did Sarika do that helped her handle the mixed feelings?
qa.a: She congratulated Irawati and then named her feeling privately to a friend, so she did not pretend it was not there.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt hearing Sarika's congratulation?
qa.a: She probably felt warm and pleased, since she beamed, and she may not have guessed Sarika was also disappointed.

grounding: A child claps and congratulates a winner while feeling disappointed, and privately names the feeling to a friend.

passage: At the district swimming gala in Pune, I sat behind Naveen and Suraj on the bleachers. Suraj had come second, and Naveen had won the race. When the results were called, Suraj sat very still and stared at his hands. Then he stood up and hugged Naveen, saying, “Great swim!” It looked a bit stiff. Later I overheard him tell his father, “I really wanted to win.” His father said, “That's fair. You can feel both.” Suraj nodded and drank his juice. I couldn't tell how long the disappointment would last, but he seemed honest about it.

qa.q: Who won the swimming race?
qa.a: Naveen.

qa.q: What did Suraj's stiff hug and quiet stare suggest about how he felt, and what else might explain them?
qa.a: They suggest he was disappointed but trying to be a good sport, though he might also have been simply tired after the race.

qa.q: What did Suraj's father do that helped?
qa.a: He said it is fair to want to win and that his son could feel both, so the feeling was named and not hidden.

qa.q: How might Naveen have seen Suraj's hug?
qa.a: Naveen may have taken it as real congratulation, or perhaps noticed the stiffness, so he could not be sure how Suraj felt.

grounding: A child congratulates the winner while disappointed, seen by an observer, and later names the feeling to a parent.

passage: Monday: The headmistress read out the essay prize winner: Kamal. Jeevan had wanted it so badly he'd rewritten his three times. He clapped with everyone, face stiff, and said, “Well done,” without looking at Kamal. At home he threw his bag on the bed. “I'm so jealous I could scream,” he told Amma. She said, “That's allowed. Say it here. You don't have to say it there.” Wednesday: Jeevan found Kamal by the water cooler. “Your ending was really good. The bit about the kite.” Kamal grinned. “Yours was close. Sir said so.” Friday: Jeevan asked Kamal how he'd thought of the kite. They talked through the whole lunch break.

qa.q: How many times had Jeevan rewritten his essay?
qa.a: Jeevan had rewritten it three times.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling as he clapped with a stiff face?
qa.a: Jeevan felt jealous and disappointed, having wanted the prize badly, but he managed to clap anyway.

qa.q: How did Amma help Jeevan handle his envy?
qa.a: She said the feeling was allowed and could be named privately at home, without having to show it to Kamal.

qa.q: How did Kamal respond to Jeevan's compliment on Wednesday?
qa.a: Kamal grinned and told Jeevan his essay had been close, which made them friends rather than rivals.

grounding: Shows a child managing envy enough to congratulate a winning friend, while naming the feeling privately at home.

passage: Jahnavi, you clapped for your friend today with a face like a closed door. Let your Sarita Mausi tell you a secret. When I was eleven, my best friend Rupa got the solo in the school choir. I had practised that song for weeks. When they announced her name, I clapped louder than anyone and smiled so hard my cheeks hurt. That night I had a stomach ache and couldn't say why. My mother sat on my bed and asked, “Are you sad about the solo?” I burst into tears. “I'm happy for Rupa. And I'm jealous. Both.” She said, “Both is honest.” The next day, clapping for Rupa felt real.

qa.q: What did Rupa get in the school choir?
qa.a: Rupa got the solo.

qa.q: What was young Sarita feeling as she clapped louder than anyone?
qa.a: She felt jealous and disappointed but hid it behind a big smile, which later came out as a stomach ache and tears.

qa.q: What choice did Sarita's mother make, and why did it help?
qa.a: She asked gently if Sarita was sad about the solo, which let her name both happiness and jealousy, making the next day's clapping real.

qa.q: How might Rupa have experienced Sarita's clapping?
qa.a: Rupa probably saw only a happy friend clapping loudly, not knowing about the hidden jealousy.

grounding: Shows a child celebrating a friend's success while hiding envy, and naming the feeling privately proving healthier than pretending.

passage: The chess final had ended in twenty minutes, and now the photographer was rushing everyone onto the stage. As runner-up, Usha had to stand beside Kamal while he held up the trophy she'd wanted all year. Her throat felt tight. There was no time to go off and be sad; the camera was already flashing. She turned, held out her hand and said, “Well played. Your knight move was brilliant.” Kamal shook it, surprised and pleased. After the photos, Usha found her coach in the corridor. “I'm really disappointed,” she said, and her voice wobbled. “Good,” said the coach. “Say it to me. And you were a proper sport up there.”

qa.q: How long did the chess final take?
qa.a: The chess final ended in twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as she stood beside Kamal on stage?
qa.a: Usha felt disappointed and tight-throated, having wanted the trophy all year.

qa.q: How did Usha manage both celebrating Kamal and her own feelings?
qa.a: She congratulated him sincerely on stage, then told her coach privately that she was really disappointed.

qa.q: How did Kamal react to Usha's handshake?
qa.a: Kamal was surprised and pleased by her sincere compliment.

grounding: Shows a child congratulating a rival who won while disappointed, then naming the feeling privately to a trusted adult.

passage:
The colony's Independence Day drawing prize went to Nilesh, for his kite-filled sky. Anand's own painting, the one he'd worked on for three evenings, didn't even get a mention. His stomach dropped. Everyone turned to look at him, because he and Nilesh were always together.

Anand made himself clap. Then he walked over and thumped Nilesh on the shoulder. "Well done, yaar. The orange kites are the best bit." Nilesh beamed.

At home, Anand sat on the kitchen stool while Mumma rolled dough. "I'm happy for him. But I really wanted it. Is that bad?"

Mumma dusted flour off her hands. "It's not bad. You felt jealous and still clapped. That's hard. Now tell me about your painting."

qa.q: What did Nilesh's winning drawing show?
qa.a: A kite-filled sky.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling as he clapped for Nilesh?
qa.a: Disappointed and a bit jealous, since his three evenings of work got no mention, yet he chose to celebrate his friend anyway.

qa.q: Why was talking to Mumma at home healthier than pretending?
qa.a: Naming the jealousy in private let Anand feel it without hiding it, and Mumma showed that feeling it and still clapping is a real skill.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel when Anand congratulates him?
qa.a: Delighted and proud, especially since his best friend praises a specific part, the orange kites.

grounding: It shows a child congratulating a friend on a prize while disappointed, and naming his envy privately to a parent rather than pretending it isn't there.
